title: Chapter 194 – Eight Children
html:
[The Council Chamber of the Sixth Door – Hai Ren]

Hai Ren decides, on the morning of the vote, that she will not cry in front of grown-ups.

It is a small resolution. She makes it the way she makes all her resolutions, in the dark before the lamps are lit, lying on her narrow bench in Qinghe's kitchen with the blanket pulled to her chin. At fourteen she has kept three promises in her life, and two of them she was too young to understand. She has no real idea what the third will cost her. She only knows that today she is going to walk into a room where people have been dying for six hundred years, and sit down in a chair, and speak.

The chair is waiting for her at the end of the Hall's lowest gallery.

It is a plain thing of black wood, round-backed and worn smooth, one of nine set in a ring around a table of unmarked stone. She has passed this room a hundred times and never once opened the door. Inside, there is no ornament, no banner, no lamp: only a round chamber with a domed ceiling, an unlit hearth, and a circle of tall windows set into the rock, looking out onto the vast breathing dark of the Hall.

"It was the Council Chamber," says Tian Mo, from the doorway. He has brought her here himself. His stone arm hangs quietly at his side. "The Nine sat in it for the last time six hundred years ago. Seven of the chairs have been empty since."

"Seven."

"Ethan's. And the Warden's. The rest were never filled."

Hai Ren looks at them. Nine chairs. In the circle of dusty light, they look smaller than she expected, and much older.

"Which one is mine?"

"That is not for me to say." The Warden's face is grave. "But I think the one that fits is the one that does not feel strange."

She walks the ring. She lays her hand on each back in turn. The first is cold and the second is rough; the third has a faint hum in the grain that makes her teeth ache. At the fifth chair her fingers stop. It is lower than the others, and the seat is worn by a smaller person than she, and when she sits, her feet reach the floor.

"This one," she says.

"I thought so."

"Who sat here?"

"No one remembers." He bows, a small formal bow with his stone hand against his breast. "But it has been waiting for you."

* * *

They come one by one, and each one finds a chair.

Cheng Hui first, nineteen and grave, who takes the one nearest the door and sits very straight with his hands on his knees. Duan Ke next, scowling, with a stick of firewood he has been told he cannot bring in. He hangs it on the back of his chair anyway. Zhen Li slips in at his heels with her nails bitten to the quick. Ao arrives on Qinghe's hip, rubbing his eyes, and is set down in a chair so large that his legs swing. Tao climbs into the seventh without help, with great dignity.

Mo Yan comes alone. She crosses the floor without a sound and settles into the sixth, and when she lifts her eyes to Hai Ren, Hai Ren sees that she has been crying and has decided, like Hai Ren, not to say so.

Cheng Hui had told her that morning, over the porridge, what the red note meant.

I have chosen eight. Seven of them are the Seven. The eighth, he said, had not been in the Roll Room: the eighth had been a Lin child too, born in the valley, whom the Warden had marked years before the rest, and set apart. A boy who had lived in the clan hall and eaten the clan's bread, and who one winter's morning, in a courtyard of snow, had woken with another man's mind in his head.

"Jian," Hai Ren had said.

"The Roll has him as the first." Cheng Hui had pushed his bowl away. "He's older than any of us. He doesn't know."

"Should we tell him?"

"He knows now. I told him last night." A pause. "He laughed for a long time. Then he said, Of course. I should have guessed. It is exactly the sort of joke the Founders would make."

Hai Ren had not laughed. She had looked at the tall, thin, bloody-lipped young man across the kitchen, who was gravely cutting a loaf into slices for the children, and thought that he had been carrying the Hall's door for six hundred years without ever being told he was a hinge.

The eighth chair is Jian's.

He is late. When he enters, leaning hard on the staff, there is an uneasy hush, and Hai Ren sees the others watch him cross the floor. He has shadows under his eyes the color of bruises. A line of dried silver runs from the corner of his left eye to his jaw, which nobody has asked him about. He lowers himself into the chair with a care that tells her what it costs, and for a moment he sits with his eyes closed, breathing.

"I'm sorry," he says. "I was with Mr. Cole."

"How is he?" asks Zhen Li.

"Sleeping. Nurse says he will wake." Jian opens his eyes. "I told her to say so, whether it is true or not."

"Is it?"

"I do not know."

Nobody speaks. The ninth chair is empty.

Then the door opens again and Mei steps into the room.

She has almost nothing left. Hai Ren sees it at once, the way one sees a candle that is guttering. Her light has gone thin and gray at the edges. The ribbon of her hair hangs limp. She walks to the ninth chair, slowly, like a woman climbing a stair, and when she sits it is with the stillness of someone who is afraid to jostle something inside her.

"Seven percent," she says, to the room at large. "I'm sorry. I'd hoped for more."

"Sit as long as you need," says Jian.

"I'm sitting." A small crooked smile. "It's the only thing I'm good at now."

* * *

It is Cheng Hui who calls them to order, in the end, because he is the eldest and nobody else will.

"There are nine of us," he says, and his voice cracks and steadies. "The old Nine took an oath that the Rest of All would not be woken except by consent of the Nine. That is what the red note says. It has been broken once already, in a small way, by the Alpha and the Veiled and the beasts. If Door Seven opens before we agree, everyone wakes at once."

"Nine million," says Zhen Li.

"Nine million, four hundred thousand."

"And there is no food for them."

"There is no food for us," says Duan Ke harshly.

Silence. The cold light shifts on the stone.

"So that is the question." Cheng Hui folds his hands. "What do we do with them? What can we do?"

Hai Ren hears the question, and under it she hears the other, the one nobody has asked, the one she asked herself at three in the morning with her face in the blanket. What do we owe them?

"I want to say something," she says.

They look at her. She is surprised how steady her voice is.

"Everyone in the Hall is asleep because someone else decided they should be," she says. "The Warden decided. Ethan decided. The Nine decided. They did it out of love, or fear, or because they were out of time. But nobody asked." She presses her palms against her knees. "I was a baby. I did not choose to be put in a bed. Mo Yan did not choose. Tao did not. We were kept, and we have all been so angry about it, and I think..." Her throat tightens. "I think if we do the same thing, if we vote to keep them asleep, or to wake them all at once, we are just doing it again."

"What's the alternative?" says Duan Ke.

"Ask them."

The word falls into the room like a stone into a well.

"Ask nine million sleepers?" says Zhen Li.

"One at a time. In the dream." Hai Ren looks at Mei. "Can we?"

Mei's gray eyes widen. She is quiet for a moment, as if listening to something far away.

"Maybe," she says slowly. "The Hall's lamps are threads. I can feel them. If the Nine hold the threads together, if we all hold them, I think... I think one of us could ask a question, and the sleeper could answer." She stops. "But it would cost."

"How much?"

"A lot. For the one who asks." She does not look away. "I'd be the one. I know them best."

"No," says Jian.

"Jian—"

"No." He leans forward, and the effort makes him cough. It takes a long moment. When he lifts his head again his lip is bloody, and he wipes it with the back of his hand, without apology. "We are the Nine. That means we share it. If this is going to cost, it will cost all of us equally, or we do not do it."

There is a pause.

"All of us," repeats Cheng Hui, thoughtfully. "A part of each."

"A small part."

"How small?"

Mei shuts her eyes. A faint line appears between her brows. "A day," she says at last. "From each of us. For each sleeper we ask. If they say yes, we wake them gently, one at a time, as fast as the Hall can feed them. If they say no..."

"Then they sleep," says Hai Ren. "Until they want to wake."

"Yes."

"And a day from each."

"From each. For every question." Mei opens her eyes. "It is not much."

"For nine million," says Duan Ke, flatly, "it's twenty-six thousand years."

* * *

The arithmetic undoes them all.

It takes a quarter of an hour, and a good deal of shouting. Duan Ke has done the sum on his fingers, and then on the stone table with a chip of coal, and then he shoves back his chair and stalks to the window. Zhen Li is crying. Tao, who has no idea what is happening, has started to hiccup.

"Quiet," says Cheng Hui. "Let me think."

"There is nothing to think about. We cannot do it."

"There must be a way to—"

"There is a way."

It is Jian who says it. The room turns. He has not moved from his chair. His eyes are closed again, and the dried silver on his face looks like tracery on porcelain, and when he speaks it is slowly, as a man speaks who is reading something off the inside of his own skull.

"A question costs a day if you ask it once. But if you ask it of all of them together, in one breath, the cost does not multiply. It is the same cost." He opens his eyes. "I have the Interface back, now. It can carry the question to every thread in the Hall at the same time. It can listen to all the answers. It can sort them, the yeses from the refusals."

"A day," says Mei, wonderingly. "One day. From each of us."

"One."

"But then—" Hai Ren's mind races. "The ones who say yes. Nine million, if they all say yes. We would still have to feed them."

"Not all at once." Jian's smile is wan. "I am told there is a way to wake a sleeper partially. To rouse them just enough to eat, to walk, to choose. And then to let them sleep again if the answer is not yet. It would take a good many years."

"Years?"

"I do not mind years." He glances around the circle, and something moves in his bruised face that Hai Ren has not seen before. It is something soft, and rueful, and entirely unafraid. "None of us here is in a hurry. We are the Nine. We have, between us, a great deal of time."

* * *

Before the vote, Mei finds Hai Ren at the window.

She comes across the floor like a leaf on still water, and stops at Hai Ren's elbow, and for a while says nothing. Outside the glass, the great dark Hall breathes. Ring on ring of lamps climbs into the vault, and a few, in the highest circle, are dark.

"Those are the ones I lost," says Mei softly. "Four hundred and twelve. And sixty-one."

"You didn't lose them. Ethan did."

"I held the door." She does not look away from the glass. "It's the same."

"It isn't."

"You're fourteen," says Mei, with a faint smile. "You can't tell me what's the same."

"I'm fourteen and I can read faster than anyone in this room." Hai Ren folds her arms. It comes out sharper than she means. "I read the Roll. Do you know what Zhao says? He says a clan is who is written down by someone who couldn't bear to leave them out."

Mei turns her head.

"I'm writing you down," says Hai Ren. Her ears are hot. "I don't care if you're a pattern. I don't care if you're a, a kept thing. You held the door when nobody asked you to. That's a Lin. That's a person. So you're written down."

Mei stares at her. Her gray eyes fill, and the light around her face trembles like a candle in a draft.

"That's the nicest thing anyone's ever said to me," she says.

"Don't tell Duan Ke. He'll say I'm soft."

"I won't." A small, wet laugh. "I promise."

They stand side by side at the window, a fourteen-year-old girl and a fading light, looking out at the dark. After a while Hai Ren feels a cool hand slip into hers, and she does not let go.

They vote, in the end, with their hands.

It is Cheng Hui's idea. He says that a spoken vote is easily bent, and that a lifted hand is a promise, and promises are all they have. He asks the question as the old Warden's note asked it, in the old Warden's words, and Hai Ren hears it ring against the domed ceiling like a bell.

"Shall the Rest of All be woken only by the consent of the Nine, each sleeper asked, each answer heard, none compelled?"

Her hand goes up first. She did not know it would. It rises on its own, the right hand with its bitten nails, and hangs in the cold light as if it belonged to someone else.

Cheng Hui lifts his. Then Mo Yan. Then Tao, with both hands, in case one is not enough. Zhen Li wipes her eyes and raises hers. Ao, on his chair, puts his hand up because everyone else has and begins to giggle. Duan Ke stands at the window with his back to them all, a thin tense figure, and for a long time he does not move.

"Duan Ke," says Cheng Hui gently.

"I'm thinking."

"Take as long as you like."

"I'm not sure." The boy turns, and his face is blotched and hard. "I'm not sure I want them awake. I'm not sure I want them to know. They'll look at us the way those kids looked at us in the yard when we first came out. Like we were something Ethan dragged in."

"They may."

"They will." His voice shakes. "And we'll be nine children holding the door for them."

"Yes," says Hai Ren.

"And if they say no?"

"Then they say no."

"And if they say yes, and they hate us?"

Hai Ren draws a breath. She had decided she would not cry. She finds, to her surprise, that she is not going to. "Then they hate us," she says. "But at least they will be here to do it."

Duan Ke stares at her. A long, odd, searching look. Then, stiffly, as if every joint hurt, he lifts his arm.

It is not quite a raised hand. It is a clenched fist, with the knuckles white. But it is up.

"Seven," says Cheng Hui softly. "Eight. Jian?"

Jian's hand has been in the air for some time. He has not said anything. He looks very tired. Then he turns to the girl in the ninth chair, small and silver and fading.

"Mei."

"I know." She smiles. It is the smile of a child who has just learned that a promise can be a gift. She lifts her thin hand, and it passes through the light, and for an instant it is almost solid.

"Nine," says Cheng Hui.

In the high dark of the Hall, a bell begins to ring.

* * *

It is not the Founders' Bell. It is smaller and sweeter, and it comes from everywhere at once: from the stone, from the roots, from the lamp-threads reaching up into the vault. It rings once, twice, three times, and each stroke goes through Hai Ren like warm water. She feels something take hold of her chest and settle, a quiet tightening, as if a ring were closing around her heart.

"The Nine," whispers Mei.

On the table, in the middle of the unmarked stone, a line of pale fire appears and runs around the whole circle, joining nine points of light. Each point is a chair. Each is a child. The fire burns without heat and without sound, and when it is finished, a tenth light rises at the center of the table, a small steady golden flame, and hangs there in the air.

"What is that?" asks Tao.

"The question," says Jian, and his voice is hoarse. He is looking at the flame. He has gone very white. "I think... I think it's waiting for us to ask."

Cheng Hui looks around the circle. He swallows.

"Together?" he says.

"Together."

They join hands. It is clumsy, nine of them around a stone table, with Ao's small damp fingers in Zhen Li's and Mei's nearly transparent palm slipping through Jian's. Hai Ren takes Mo Yan's hand on her left and Duan Ke's fist on her right, and he opens it, grudgingly, and lets her hold it.

"Say it," says Mei.

"Who wants to wake?" asks Hai Ren, in a voice that is steadier than she has ever heard it.

The flame blazes up. And the whole Hall answers.

* * *

It is not a sound. It is a flood.

It comes through the soles of her feet and the crown of her head, a vast rising tide of voices, each so quiet that it is almost nothing, and all together so enormous that she cannot breathe. She hears a woman laugh. She hears a child ask for her mother. She hears an old man say, Is it morning? She hears a hundred thousand voices say yes, and a hundred thousand say no, and a hundred thousand more say I don't know and wait and please, a little longer. She hears a man weeping with relief. She hears a girl, no older than Tao, whisper Mama? to a dark that has been very long.

She is aware that her knees have given way. She is aware that Duan Ke's hand is crushing her fingers. She is aware of a bright pain behind her eyes like a lantern being lit in a dark room, and of someone saying her name, over and over, with an urgent hoarse tenderness. Hai Ren. Hai Ren. Hai Ren.

It stops.

The silence afterward is like a blow. For a long moment nobody can speak. Hai Ren lies on the stone floor with her cheek against the cold, and the whole chamber spins slowly around her. She can feel the day leave her, a faint cool tug, like a thread drawn out of cloth. She is a little thinner. She is a little older.

She is not sorry.

"How many?" whispers Cheng Hui.

Jian is sitting upright in his chair, rigid, with blood running from his nose. His eyes are fixed on the middle distance. He is reading something no one else can see; she has learned not to ask what.

"Four million, two hundred thousand said yes," he says. "Two million, nine hundred thousand said no, and I have marked each of them to sleep undisturbed. The rest..." He laughs, a cracked, astonished sound. "The rest said not yet."

"Four million," says Zhen Li. "Four million."

"Not all at once. Never all at once." Jian wipes his nose, looks at the blood on his hand, and does not seem to care. "The Hall can wake a thousand a month, with the grain we have. Two thousand, if Han's measures arrive. Perhaps ten thousand a month once the Wall's harvest is in."

"Then it'll take..."

"A long while." He turns his head, slowly, and for the first time since the chamber door opened, he smiles with his whole face. "But we will do it the right way."

* * *

The first sleeper wakes at dusk.

They carry her down on a litter, six of them, with Tian Mo at the head. She is in her sixties, perhaps, a stout gray woman in a quilted gown who was lying in the third ring when the Hall's lamp flickered, and who said, in the instant before the flood, a single word. The word was not yes. It was a name.

Qinghe has made soup. It is the only thing she knows to make. She sits at the end of the long table, with the black kettle at her elbow, and when the woman opens her eyes, Qinghe is the first thing she sees.

"Hello," says Qinghe.

The woman blinks. Her eyes are slow, and gray, and bewildered. She looks at the kitchen, at the rafters, at the row of children along the bench, small faces watching her with the tense hope of people who have never before been the cause of anything good.

"Where am I?" she says. Her voice is a rasp.

"You're in my kitchen," says Qinghe. "You've been asleep. You were asked a question, and you said you'd like to wake up. Do you remember?"

The woman frowns. "I remember... a tree. A song." She blinks. "Somebody called me. A little girl. She asked if I wanted to come home."

"That was Mei."

"Mei." The old woman turns her head, searching. "Is she here?"

Hai Ren, sitting beside Mo Yan on the bench, feels her heart turn over. She looks toward the corner by the stove where a small pale shape, thin as breath, is leaning against the wall.

"I'm here," whispers Mei.

The old woman looks at her for a long moment. Then something happens to her face, a slow dawning softness, and she holds out one weathered hand.

"Come here, child. Let me see you."

Mei crosses the floor. It takes her a long time. She stops in front of the stout old woman, and the woman reaches out and lays her palm against the child's cheek, and the light shivers, and holds.

"You look just like her," says the old woman.

"Like who?"

"Lena." The old woman smiles through her tears. "I was her neighbor. The one with the cat. She used to say you would grow up to be braver than all of us."

The kitchen goes very quiet.

Hai Ren cannot look at Mei. She looks instead at the soup, at the steam curling up, and at the small gold flame she can still feel in her chest, where the Nine's ring is closed. She thinks: four million, two hundred thousand. She thinks: one at a time.

She thinks, with a clarity that surprises her: this is what a clan is.

On the table, by the black kettle, a bowl of barley and turnip sits in a ring of lamplight, and someone has remembered to put a spoon beside it.
